title: Association between dental pulp necroptosis-related signaling and elodont incisor growth retardation in hyperglycemic rats.
byline: Kim MG, Ben Amara H, Thomsen P, et al.
html:
Introduction: Although type 1 diabetes (T1D) induces systemic allostatic load, whether sustained hyperglycemia is accompanied by necroptosis-related signaling within the dental pulp (DP) niche and its impact on the developmental kinetics of continuously growing elodont incisors remains unclear.

Objectives: This study investigated whether sustained hyperglycemia was accompanied by enhanced RIPK3-MLKL necroptosis-related signaling within the DP niche and whether these molecular alterations coincided with attenuation of elodont incisor growth.

Methods: T1D was induced in Sprague-Dawley rats using streptozotocin (65 mg/kg). Systemic metabolic profiles, necroptotic markers in serum/dental tissues (immunohistochemistry, ELISA, and Western blotting), and mandibular incisor growth (a standardized notch-creation method for 49 days) were evaluated. Group differences were assessed primarily using two-sided Welch's t-tests, with exact Mann-Whitney U tests for sensitivity analyses, while discriminative performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC-AUC) and precision-recall (PR curve-based AP) analyses.

Results: Hyperglycemic rats exhibited impaired weight gain, systemic inflammatory induction (elevated NLR/MLR), and elevated hepatic stress markers. Molecular profiling demonstrated increased oxidative damage (4-HNE) and necroptosis-related molecular alterations in dental tissues and DP-derived cells. Incisor growth rates differed significantly at the Phase-Transition (0.532 vs. 0.400 mm/day; Welch's p = 0.024), reaching definitive retardation in Phase-2 (0.594 vs. 0.408 mm/day; p < 0.001). Discriminatory performance improved from the Phase-Transition (ROC-AUC = 0.693; AP = 0.784) to Phase-2 (ROC-AUC = 1.000; AP = 1.000). Glycemic reversion was accompanied by normalization of necroptosis-related markers and incisor growth kinetics.

Conclusion: Hyperglycemia-induced incisor growth retardation is associated with increased oxidative stress, altered PGAM5 expression, and enhanced RIPK3-MLKL necroptosis-related signaling in dental tissues and DP-derived cells. Translationally, longitudinal evaluation of elodont incisor growth kinetics could serve as a minimally invasive phenotypic indicator of metabolic dysregulation in preclinical diabetic models and support refinement under the 3Rs principle.
